Cantor's Theorem

See that any set is smaller than the collection of all its subsets. Flip a list's diagonal to build a new element.

The power set collects all subsets. One extra element doubles the subsets. So any attempted pairing leaves leftovers. The diagonal-flipped set is exactly such a leftover.

For example, three 🧑 classmates have eight subsets. Subsets already outnumber the friends. More people only widens the gap. Even infinity keeps the gap.

  3. y∈(0,1)y \in (0,1)y∈(0,1): 0.444…≤y≤0.555…0.444\ldots \le y \le 0.555\ldots0.444…≤y≤0.555….

    If y=xny = x_ny=xn​, then since the decimal expansion of yyy contains no 000 or 999, it cannot have an alternative expansion — two decimal expansions of the same number can differ only when one ends in infinite 000s and the other in infinite 999s — so the expansion of yyy is unique.

    Hence the nnn-th digit of xnx_nxn​ must be ene_nen​, contradicting en≠dnne_n \ne d_{nn}en​=dnn​.

    Hence (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) is not countable: it is uncountable.

    QED.
